stimulus.directions: Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it.

paragraphs: The conventional case for cheap credit is straightforward: when borrowing costs fall, firms invest, households spend, and an economy emerging from a slump regains momentum. This logic is sound as far as it goes, but it quietly assumes that the funds released by lower rates find their way to productive uses. Experience suggests that this assumption holds only when lenders can distinguish promising borrowers from merely persistent ones. Where rates remain low for years, that discrimination erodes. A bank earning thin margins on new loans has every incentive to keep renewing old ones, because recognising a bad loan means admitting a loss, whereas rolling it over merely postpones the accounting.

The consequence is a population of what economists sometimes call zombie firms: enterprises that earn just enough to service their interest but never enough to repay principal or fund expansion. Individually they are harmless, even sympathetic, since they preserve jobs. Collectively, however, they occupy markets, labour and credit that more dynamic competitors could use. A start-up that cannot obtain a loan because the lender's appetite is committed elsewhere is a cost that never appears in any ledger, which is precisely why it is so rarely counted. Their persistence also blurs the signals on which healthy markets depend, since a sector crowded with firms that should have exited appears busier than it really is. Defenders of prolonged easy money reply that the alternative, a wave of closures in a fragile economy, would be worse. That reply deserves respect, but it treats the choice as a binary one between forbearance and collapse, when the real alternative is gradual, supervised restructuring.

None of this proves that low interest rates are a mistake. In a deep recession, the damage from tight credit can be far larger and less reversible than any distortion that cheap money produces. The argument is narrower: the benefits of easy credit diminish with duration, while its hidden costs accumulate. A policy that is wise as an emergency measure may become unwise as a permanent condition, and the difficulty lies in recognising the moment when one has turned into the other. Regulators who insist on honest loan classification, and who require banks to set aside provisions early, do not oppose growth; they protect the mechanism through which growth is financed. The remedy is hardly mysterious, only unwelcome, because it asks lenders and borrowers alike to accept modest losses now in exchange for sounder gains later.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?
options: Start-ups contribute more to economic recovery than established firms and ought to be given priority in lending.
Banks rather than regulators are chiefly responsible for the survival of firms that can no longer repay their loans.
The conventional case for easy credit is mistaken, as lower rates never lead firms to invest or households to spend more.
Low interest rates should be abandoned, since they inevitably produce zombie firms and stifle new enterprise in every sector.
Cheap credit loses much of its value when prolonged, since lending quality declines and hidden costs build up.
questions.explanation: The passage argues that easy credit helps at first but that its benefits "diminish with duration" while hidden costs accumulate. It explicitly denies that low rates are simply a mistake, and it does not blame banks alone.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred about a bank that keeps renewing the loans of struggling borrowers?
options: It will cause every start-up in its area to fail, since no credit at all remains available to them.
It has broken the lending rules and will be forced by regulators to close down within a few years of the practice being discovered.
It is probably tying up credit that newer, promising firms could use, while delaying the recording of losses.
It earns larger margins on renewed loans than on new loans, which explains why it prefers to renew them rather than lend afresh.
It is certain to recover the principal in full once interest rates eventually return to a higher level.
questions.explanation: Rolling over a loan "postpones the accounting" of a loss, and zombie borrowers occupy credit that others could use. Taken together, the two points support the keyed statement; the passage gives no basis for the claims of certain recovery, higher margins, illegality or universal start-up failure.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred about the author's view of cheap credit as time passes?
options: Cheap credit should be withdrawn at the first sign that a recession is coming to an end, whatever the state of banks.
The harm caused by tight credit is always smaller than the distortion that cheap money produces, however deep the recession.
The merits of a policy depend only on its original purpose and not at all on how long the policy lasts.
Emergency measures should never be adopted, because they are bound to become permanent and to damage lending quality.
A policy defensible in a severe downturn may deserve less support as it continues, since gains fade and costs grow.
questions.explanation: The author says tight credit in a deep recession can do greater damage than cheap money, yet that the benefits of easy credit "diminish with duration" while hidden costs accumulate. Combining these gives the keyed view, and the other statements reverse or exaggerate the author's position.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about how lending to zombie firms is usually judged?
options: It looks harmless because the jobs saved are visible, while the opportunities denied to other firms simply go uncounted.
It is judged accurately, because economists enter the loans refused to start-ups in detailed ledgers.
It is judged mainly by the interest that zombie firms pay, rather than by the number of jobs that they preserve.
It is judged harshly, because the closures it prevents are always easy to measure and to record in official accounts.
It is judged favourably only by defenders of easy money, who admit that it distorts the market for credit.
questions.explanation: Zombie firms are described as "harmless, even sympathetic, since they preserve jobs", whereas the start-up that is refused credit is a cost that "never appears in any ledger". The two sentences together explain why the lending looks more benign than it is.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE according to the passage?
options: Zombie firms are described as unable to meet even the interest due on their borrowings from banks.
Banks with thin margins on new loans are described as keen to recognise bad loans promptly and in full.
A firm able to pay its interest may still lack the earnings to repay its debt or expand.
Regulators who demand early provisions are described as opponents of economic growth in general.
Defenders of prolonged easy money are said to have overlooked the risk of widespread closures in a fragile economy.
questions.explanation: Zombie firms earn "just enough to service their interest but never enough to repay principal or fund expansion". The other statements reverse what the passage says about zombie firms, the defenders, banks and regulators.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true according to the passage?
options: Those who favour long periods of easy money fear that a wave of closures would damage a fragile economy.
The skill of lenders in telling promising borrowers from merely persistent ones can weaken when rates stay low for years.
The author regards honest loan classification by regulators as an obstacle to growth.
The harm done to a start-up that cannot obtain credit is rarely entered in any formal record.
The author proposes gradual, supervised restructuring as an alternative to indefinite forbearance.
questions.explanation: The author says regulators who insist on honest classification "do not oppose growth; they protect the mechanism through which growth is financed", so the keyed statement contradicts the passage. The remaining statements are all supported by it.

questions.stem: The tone of the passage can best be described as:
questions.explanation: The author weighs the case for cheap credit, concedes its value in a recession, and warns about the costs of prolonging it. That is analytical and cautionary rather than purely descriptive, angry, resigned or approving.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most similar in meaning to the word “forbearance” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: As used in "a binary one between forbearance and collapse", forbearance means refraining from enforcing losses and tolerating weak borrowers, which is closest to leniency.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most opposite in meaning to the word “dynamic” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: In "more dynamic competitors", dynamic means energetic and growing, so stagnant is its opposite; the other words are close in sense to dynamic.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to be true, judging only from the passage?
options: Start-ups never need bank loans as long as existing firms use their credit productively and in good time.
A bank forced to classify loans honestly may show lower profits for a time than one that keeps renewing them.
Banks that renew doubtful loans are always unaware of the losses that they are busy postponing.
Zombie firms would at once become profitable if interest rates were raised even by a small margin this year.
Regulators who demand early provisions would also prefer that interest rates stay low indefinitely, whatever the effect on banks.
questions.explanation: Recognising a bad loan "means admitting a loss", and regulators require honest classification and early provisions, so a bank that complies is likely to show lower profits in the short run. The other statements have no support in the passage or run against it.

stimulus.directions: Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it.

paragraphs: Whenever a society decides that something valuable ought to be improved, it tends to begin by measuring it. The impulse is reasonable, since what cannot be measured can scarcely be managed, and the early years of a measurement scheme often do yield genuine gains. No parent, after all, would choose a doctor whose results nobody had ever checked. Schools that must publish their examination results, for instance, are pressed to ask why some classrooms lag behind, and neglected pupils sometimes receive overdue attention. The difficulty arises later, when the measure ceases to be a window onto the activity and becomes its purpose.

Once teachers' reputations, funding and promotions hinge on a score, rational behaviour shifts. Time flows towards topics that are tested and away from those that are not; pupils are drilled in the format of questions rather than in the ideas those questions were designed to probe. A teacher who spends a week on a poem that will not appear in the examination is, in effect, risking a penalty for the sake of her pupils. The scores rise, and by the narrow standard of the scheme the schools improve. Yet the rise may reflect skill at the test itself rather than any deeper understanding, and the indicator, having been optimised, no longer indicates what it once did. Nor is this primarily a matter of dishonesty. Most educators who teach to the test do so reluctantly, aware of the loss, but they are responding sensibly to the incentives they have been handed.

It would be a mistake to conclude that measurement should be abandoned. Without evidence, decisions about schooling would be driven by anecdote and prejudice, and the pupils with the least influential advocates would suffer most. Both extremes, blind trust in numbers and wholesale distrust of them, fail the very pupils they claim to serve. A wiser course is to treat every metric as provisional, to use several measures in combination so that no single figure can be gamed, and to reserve a measure of judgement for those who observe pupils directly. Judgement, admittedly, is open to favouritism, which is why it should supplement the numbers and not replace them. A score is a useful servant of understanding but a poor master. When it is permitted to rule, the activity it was meant to illuminate is slowly rearranged to suit it.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the passage?
options: Why Examination Results Should Be Published by Every School Nationwide
The Dishonesty of Teachers Under Pressure to Perform Well
How Pupils Can Be Drilled Successfully for Examination Questions Quickly
When the Measure Becomes the Goal: Limits of Scoring
Abandoning Measurement: The Case for Judgement Alone in Schools
questions.explanation: The passage traces how a measure that starts as a useful window on schooling becomes the aim itself, while still defending measurement in moderation. The other titles are too narrow, reverse the author's stance or ignore the central warning.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the early years of a measurement scheme in schools?
options: Its neglected pupils receive attention only after the measure has become the purpose of schooling.
Its gains are usually larger than those that the same scheme produces in its later years.
Its gains are genuine, because the measure still reflects the activity before incentives distort it.
Its main effect is to make teachers resist any form of public reporting of examination results.
Its apparent benefits are mostly statistical illusions that vanish once schools publish their results.
questions.explanation: Early on, schemes "often do yield genuine gains", and the trouble "arises later, when the measure ceases to be a window onto the activity". The two statements together imply that the early gains are real because the measure has not yet become the target.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why many teachers teach to the test?
options: They are indifferent to understanding so long as the funding for their school improves.
They respond sensibly to rewards tied to scores, though they regret the loss of learning.
They believe that skill in test technique matters more than deeper understanding of a subject.
They doubt that any reliable evidence about the progress of pupils can ever be gathered.
They have been instructed by examiners to ignore any topic that does not appear in the test.
questions.explanation: Reputations, funding and promotions "hinge on a score", and most educators teach to the test "reluctantly, aware of the loss", responding "sensibly to the incentives". The passage therefore presents the behaviour as rational but regretted.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a reason, implied in the passage, for using several measures together?
options: Several measures cost less to collect than a single examination score, which suits most schools.
Several measures remove the need for any human judgement in assessing pupils, however carefully chosen.
A combination of measures makes teachers stop feeling reluctant about testing, since scores matter less.
Different measures let each school choose whichever one flatters it most, and so appear to improve.
A single figure on which rewards depend invites narrow optimisation, whereas several are much harder to game.
questions.explanation: Once a single score decides rewards, teaching bends towards it and the indicator stops indicating. Using "several measures in combination" is recommended "so that no single figure can be gamed", which supports the keyed reason; the author also keeps a role for direct judgement.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE according to the passage?
options: Measurement schemes are said to bring benefits only after several years of operation.
Publishing examination results is said to have harmed neglected pupils in the early years.
Abandoning all measurement would leave pupils lacking influential advocates most exposed.
Teachers who teach to the test are described as acting mainly out of dishonesty.
Rising scores under a high-stakes scheme reliably show deeper understanding among pupils.
questions.explanation: The author warns that without evidence decisions would rest on anecdote and prejudice, and "the pupils with the least influential advocates would suffer most". The other statements contradict the passage.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true according to the passage?
options: Most teachers who teach to the test remain unaware that anything is being lost.
Teachers may give less time to subjects that are not tested when scores determine rewards.
A metric that has been optimised may stop indicating what it once indicated.
The author thinks that every metric should be regarded as provisional.
A score is described as useful when it serves understanding but harmful when it dominates.
questions.explanation: The passage says that most such educators act "reluctantly, aware of the loss", so the keyed statement is false. The other statements restate points the author makes.

questions.stem: The author's attitude towards teachers who teach to the test is best described as:
options: Sympathetic, though critical of the system
questions.explanation: The author says the behaviour is not primarily dishonest and is a sensible response to incentives, while blaming the system that produces it. That is sympathy for the teachers combined with criticism of the system.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most similar in meaning to the word “illuminate” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: In "the activity it was meant to illuminate", illuminate means to shed light on, which is closest to clarify.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most opposite in meaning to the word “genuine” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: Genuine gains are real ones; the opposite is spurious, meaning false or only apparent.

stimulus.directions: Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it.

paragraphs: It is tempting to believe that the surest route to conserving a resource is to use it more efficiently. A household that installs a tap delivering the same wash with half the water, or a factory that adopts a process requiring less energy per unit, seems to have taken a step that benefits everyone. Policy makers like the idea for a further reason: the saving appears to arrive without asking anyone to change a habit. And in the short run it has. But efficiency also lowers the effective price of the service that the resource provides, and cheaper services tend to be consumed more freely. Part of the saving is therefore spent, in effect, on additional use.

Economists call this the rebound effect, and its size varies widely. Where demand is close to saturation, as with heating a room that is already at a comfortable temperature, little of the saving is clawed back. Where demand is elastic, as with travel or irrigation, the rebound can be large, and in unusual cases it can exceed the saving altogether, so that total consumption actually rises. Efficiency, in other words, is a necessary condition for conservation but not a sufficient one. A technology cannot, by itself, guarantee that a resource conserved per unit will be conserved in total, because the people who use it remain free to respond to what it makes cheaper. Measuring the effect is difficult, because the gain in one household may be spent on a different resource altogether, and it is the sum across a whole economy that matters.

This does not make efficiency standards pointless; a partial rebound still leaves a net gain, and the alternative of wasteful devices is hardly attractive. What the rebound effect counsels is humility about forecasting. Planners who project savings by multiplying the number of efficient devices by their per-unit economy are ignoring the behaviour of the people who use them. Policies that pair efficiency standards with a price signal, such as a charge that rises with consumption, address that behaviour directly and keep the incentive to economise alive. Such charges are seldom popular, which is why they are so often postponed in favour of standards that seem to demand nothing of consumers. Without such a complement, a society may find that it has become admirably efficient and no more frugal than before.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
options: The Case Against Charging for Water and Energy Use
Why Greater Efficiency Alone May Not Reduce Total Consumption
Why Inefficient Devices Should Be Banned Outright in Factories
The Rising Cost of Efficient Household Appliances and Devices
Irrigation and Travel: Two Resources Under Heavy Strain
questions.explanation: The passage explains that efficiency lowers the effective price of a service and so invites extra use, which can offset much of the saving. The other titles concern topics that are either peripheral or contrary to the author's argument.

questions.stem: Which of the following would the author expect to show the weakest rebound effect after an efficiency improvement?
options: A factory whose output grows because the energy for each unit has become cheaper
A farm that begins to irrigate extra land once pumping becomes cheaper
A commuter who starts travelling longer distances because each kilometre costs less
Lighting in a workshop that is already lit to the level its workers want
A household that begins running its taps for longer since each wash needs less water
questions.explanation: Rebound is small where demand is "close to saturation" and large where demand is elastic, as with travel or irrigation. A workshop already lit as people wish has little room to consume more, whereas each of the other cases involves demand that can expand when the service gets cheaper.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred about a society that adopts efficiency standards but adds no price signal?
options: Its total consumption will certainly rise above the level that it had before the standards were introduced.
Its efficiency standards will have been pointless, since users will spend every saving on extra use.
Its planners' projections of savings will prove accurate, because devices behave in a predictable way for all users.
Its households will use their devices less often because each device is more efficient than before.
Its total consumption may fall by less than the per-unit savings suggest, depending on user response.
questions.explanation: Efficiency lowers the effective price of a service, so some of the saving is spent on extra use, and without a complementary price signal that behaviour is left unchecked. Total savings may therefore fall short of the per-unit figure, but the passage says a net gain usually remains and that rises in total use occur only in unusual cases.

questions.stem: What can be concluded about a forecast that multiplies the number of efficient devices by their per-unit savings?
options: It is likely to overstate the saving, because it omits how users change their behaviour.
It is reliable whenever demand for the service in question is elastic and prices are stable.
It is likely to understate the saving, because efficient devices last longer than expected in practice.
It overestimates the number of efficient devices that people will actually choose to buy.
It is accurate for households but misleading for factories, farms and other large users.
questions.explanation: Such planners "are ignoring the behaviour of the people who use them", and that behaviour (the rebound) claws back part of the saving. A forecast that omits it will therefore tend to overstate the saving.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE according to the passage?
options: The author denies that efficiency brings any benefit even in the short run.
Efficiency standards are described as unnecessary wherever a price signal is in place.
In unusual cases, the rebound can be large enough for total consumption to rise.
The rebound effect is greatest where demand for a service is already close to saturation.
The author recommends replacing efficiency standards with a charge that rises with consumption.
questions.explanation: The passage states that "in unusual cases" the rebound can exceed the saving "so that total consumption actually rises". The other statements reverse or distort the author's claims.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true according to the passage?
options: A partial rebound still leaves a net saving of the resource overall.
Efficiency lowers the effective price of the service that a resource provides to those who use it.
The author considers efficiency standards pointless because every saving is spent on extra use.
A charge that rises with consumption keeps the incentive to economise alive for users.
The size of the rebound effect varies widely from one kind of service to another.
questions.explanation: The author says outright that the rebound "does not make efficiency standards pointless" because a partial rebound "still leaves a net gain". The keyed statement therefore contradicts the passage.

questions.stem: The author's attitude towards efficiency policy can best be described as:
questions.explanation: The author supports efficiency standards, noting a net gain remains, but insists they need a price signal and realistic forecasts. That is endorsement with reservations.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most similar in meaning to the word “counsels” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: In "What the rebound effect counsels is humility", counsels means advises or recommends.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most opposite in meaning to the word “wasteful” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: Wasteful devices squander resources; the opposite is economical, meaning sparing in use of resources.

stimulus.directions: Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it.

paragraphs: Payment technology has spent two decades removing friction. Where a purchase once required counting out notes, or at least signing a slip, it now requires a glance or a tap, and the benefits of this speed are real: queues shorten, small merchants gain customers, and the cost of handling cash falls. Merchants prize the speed too, because a customer who does not fumble for change is a customer who returns. No sensible account of digital payments can ignore these gains. But convenience is seldom neutral, and the very smoothness that makes a payment pleasant may also change what a payment means.

Behavioural researchers have long observed that people feel the loss of money more sharply when they hand over physical cash than when they pay by card, and sharper still than when a balance is merely adjusted on a screen. This sensation, sometimes called the pain of paying, acts as an unconscious brake on spending. Remove it and the brake weakens. Designers often describe a good payment experience as one that the customer barely notices. That ambition is understandable, but it deserves scrutiny: a transaction that is barely noticed is also barely remembered, and what is not remembered is hard to budget for. It does not follow that every user of a digital wallet becomes a spendthrift; many are disciplined, and some track every transaction more closely than they ever tracked cash. The claim is statistical rather than universal: across large populations, easier payment is likely to nudge average spending upwards, particularly on small and frequent purchases whose individual cost seems trivial.

If so, the responsibility for restoring a measure of friction cannot rest entirely on individuals, as though each were designing a private defence against a system built to be seamless. Providers could, for instance, offer optional spending summaries, delay-before-confirmation settings for large payments, or clear running totals within the application. Such features cost little and respect user choice. Nothing here requires hostility towards the technology; a provider that added a pause before a large transfer would not be distrusting its customers, only reminding them that the money is theirs. Critics will object that such features undermine the very convenience that customers value; yet convenience that the user can tune is a better product than convenience imposed on everyone. The aim is not to make payments laborious, but to ensure that a payment that is easy is still noticed.

questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the central point of the passage?
options: Small merchants gain more from digital payments than consumers do, which is why providers promote them so widely in most markets.
Cash should return as the main means of payment because digital wallets turn their users into spendthrifts everywhere.
Digital payments bring real gains, but their ease may weaken restraints on spending, so some friction merits restoring.
Providers alone, and not users, are to blame for the overspending seen in digital economies today.
Researchers have proved that people who pay by card always spend more than those who pay in cash do.
questions.explanation: The author grants the gains of digital payments, argues that removing friction may loosen the brake on spending, and proposes optional features to restore some friction. The other statements are extreme, unsupported or shift the blame.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred about paying from a screen balance compared with paying in cash?
options: It is felt as sharply as handing over notes, so it restrains spending to the same degree.
It is chosen mainly by people who already spend less than the average shopper does.
It is likely to be felt as a smaller loss, so it restrains spending less.
It raises spending by exactly the same amount for every user, whatever their personal habits are.
It makes every user track spending far more closely than cash ever did, in every kind of purchase.
questions.explanation: Loss is felt most sharply with cash and "sharper still" than with a screen adjustment, and the pain of paying acts as a brake on spending. A screen balance therefore brakes spending less; the passage explicitly says not every user is affected in the same way.

questions.stem: What can be concluded from the author's remark that many wallet users are disciplined?
options: Such users do not contradict a claim that concerns average behaviour in large populations.
Such users show that the pain of paying has no real effect on spending at all, for anyone.
Such users would gain nothing from optional spending summaries or clear running totals.
Such users are rare, which is why the effect on average spending across populations is small.
Such users spend more on small and frequent purchases than undisciplined users do.
questions.explanation: The author calls the claim "statistical rather than universal", about average spending across large populations, and adds that disciplined users exist. Together these show that disciplined users are consistent with the claim.

questions.stem: Which of the following would the author most probably say about a delay-before-confirmation setting for large payments?
options: It should replace running totals, which add cost to providers without respecting user choice.
It would lower the costs of merchants by reducing the number of small purchases.
It is harmful, since convenience is the only quality that customers value in any payment.
It should be compulsory for all users, because they cannot be trusted to manage their own money.
It is better offered as an adjustable option than imposed as a requirement on everyone.
questions.explanation: Such settings are listed among "optional" features that "respect user choice", and the author prefers convenience "that the user can tune" to convenience "imposed on everyone". The keyed statement follows from combining these two points.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE according to the passage?
options: The author reports that providers have already introduced features to restore friction.
Digital payments have made the handling of cash more expensive for small merchants.
Easier payment is most likely to push up spending on small, frequent purchases.
The author regards convenience as neutral in its effect on how people see money.
Researchers claim that everyone who uses a digital wallet eventually overspends.
questions.explanation: The author says easier payment is likely to raise average spending "particularly on small and frequent purchases". The other statements contradict the passage or add claims it does not make.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true according to the passage?
options: Critics may say that such features reduce the convenience that customers value so highly.
The author argues that individuals alone should be responsible for restoring friction.
Some wallet users monitor their transactions more closely than they once monitored cash.
The author expects features that restore friction to be inexpensive for providers to add.
Faster payment has helped to shorten queues at shops and to attract customers to merchants.
questions.explanation: The author says responsibility "cannot rest entirely on individuals", so the keyed statement contradicts the passage. The other statements all appear in the text.

questions.stem: The tone of the passage is best described as:
questions.explanation: The author credits digital payments, identifies a risk, answers critics and offers practical suggestions. This is balanced and constructive rather than nostalgic, alarmed, clinical or doubtful.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most similar in meaning to the word “trivial” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: In "whose individual cost seems trivial", trivial means of little importance, which is closest to insignificant.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most opposite in meaning to the word “disciplined” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: Disciplined users control their spending; the opposite is reckless, meaning lacking restraint.

stimulus.directions: Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions given below it.

paragraphs: Many young adults take their first job with a clear idea of what they want to buy but little idea of how to manage what they earn. Schools teach algebra and history, yet very few teach how a salary slip is read, how interest works, or why a small debt can grow quickly if it is left unpaid. As a result, many people learn about money the hard way, through mistakes that cost them dearly.

A simple habit can prevent many of these mistakes: saving a fixed portion of income as soon as it arrives, before spending anything. Those who wait to see what is left at the end of the month often find that nothing is left. Saving first turns the habit into a rule, and a rule is easier to follow than a good intention. Even a small amount, put aside regularly, grows over the years, particularly when it earns interest, because the interest itself starts to earn more interest.

Credit cards deserve special care. They are useful for emergencies and for buying things that can be repaid within a month, but they charge high interest on unpaid balances. A person who pays only the minimum amount each month may stay in debt for years while paying much more than the original price. The sensible approach is to treat a card as a convenience, not as extra income.

None of this requires advanced knowledge. What it requires is the early habit of asking three questions before any large purchase: Do I need it? Can I pay for it without borrowing? What will I give up if I buy it? Young adults who learn to ask these questions are far better prepared for the financial decisions that lie ahead, and teaching such habits in schools could help them to begin sooner.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Credit cards are so dangerous that young people should never use them at all.
Young adults earn too little to be able to save anything on a regular basis.
Interest is the single most important thing that a young person must understand.
Schools should replace algebra and history with lessons about banking, loans and taxes.
Simple, early money habits can help young adults avoid costly financial mistakes.
questions.explanation: The passage describes habits such as saving first, using credit carefully and asking questions before buying, all aimed at preventing costly mistakes. The other statements are extreme or cover only a small part of the passage.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred about a person who saves only what is left at the end of the month?
options: That person is certain to end up in debt within a few years of starting work.
That person is likely to save little, as saving then rests on intention, not a fixed rule.
That person will save more than someone who saves first, because spending becomes more careful.
That person has probably avoided all use of credit cards and the interest they charge.
That person earns interest on a larger sum than other savers do over the years.
questions.explanation: Those who wait "often find that nothing is left", and saving first works because "a rule is easier to follow than a good intention". Together these suggest that saving what remains depends on intention and tends to produce little.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about someone who pays only the minimum amount on a credit card each month?
options: The person will clear the debt more quickly than someone who pays the full balance each month.
The total paid may end up far above the price of the goods, as interest keeps being added.
The person will pay no interest as long as the minimum is paid on time each month.
The person is using the card correctly for emergencies, exactly as the passage advises.
The person's debt will disappear after one year, whatever the original price of the goods was.
questions.explanation: Cards "charge high interest on unpaid balances", and paying only the minimum may keep a person in debt for years while paying "much more than the original price". The keyed statement combines these two points.

questions.stem: Why do many people learn about money only through costly mistakes?
options: Money management is seldom taught in schools, so they learn its rules only after errors.
Salaries are generally too low to allow any careful planning of income and spending.
Algebra and history are taught in a way that confuses students about how interest works.

Young adults usually refuse advice from older relatives about how to handle money.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE according to the passage?

Interest earned on savings can itself go on to earn further interest over the years.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true according to the passage?

The author advises young adults to avoid credit cards altogether.
Teaching about money in schools could help young people to begin learning earlier.
Three questions should be asked before any large purchase is made.
Credit cards are useful for emergencies and for purchases repaid within a month.
questions.explanation: The author calls cards useful for emergencies and for purchases repaid quickly, and recommends treating them as a convenience, so advising total avoidance contradicts the passage. The other statements are all in the text.

questions.stem: The tone of the passage is best described as:
questions.explanation: The author offers practical habits and closes with a hopeful note about being better prepared. That is advisory and encouraging rather than stern, uninvolved, doubtful or gloomy.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most similar in meaning to the word “sensible” as used in the passage?

paragraphs: When online shopping first spread, many predicted that small local shops would disappear within a few years. A decade later, the picture is more complicated. Some shops did close, especially those that sold products that are easy to compare and ship, such as books and basic electronics. But many others have survived, and a few have even grown, by doing things that a website finds hard to do.

The first advantage is trust built over time. A shopkeeper who has served the same families for years knows what each customer likes and can suggest products without being asked. A buyer can also see and touch the goods, and this matters most for clothes, furniture and food, where quality is difficult to judge from a photograph. The second advantage is speed in a particular sense: although online orders can arrive in a day or two, a local shop can hand over the goods at once. A third is flexibility. A neighbourhood store may allow a regular customer to pay at the end of the month, or to return an item without any fuss.

Yet it would be wrong to say that local retailers have nothing to fear. Online platforms can offer lower prices because they sell in huge volumes, and they never close. Shops that ignore these facts risk losing younger customers, who are used to comparing prices on a phone before they walk in. The most successful local retailers have therefore chosen to cooperate with technology instead of resisting it. They accept digital payments, take orders by messaging, and offer home delivery within their own area.
The lesson is that technology rarely destroys an entire kind of business; it changes the way in which the business must compete.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best title for the passage?
options: Home Delivery: The Future of Every Neighbourhood Store
Books and Electronics: Products That Are Easy to Ship and Compare
How Local Shops Survive by Mixing Strengths with Technology
Why Online Platforms Charge Lower Prices Than Local Stores
The Decline of Local Shops in the Age of Online Shopping
questions.explanation: The passage explains how local shops have survived by using their own strengths and by cooperating with technology. The other titles focus on a single detail or suggest a decline that the passage does not describe.

questions.stem: Which kind of shop is most at risk from online sellers, according to the passage?
options: A shop selling standard goods that can be judged from a description
A shop that offers home delivery and takes orders by messaging
A shop selling clothes to buyers who value being able to try them on
A shop selling food to families who have known the owner for years
A shop selling furniture that customers wish to touch before buying
questions.explanation: The shops that closed sold goods "easy to compare and ship", while quality is hard to judge online for clothes, furniture and food. A shop selling standard goods that need no inspection is therefore the most exposed.

questions.stem: Why might a local shop lose younger customers?
options: They believe that local owners do not really know their customers or their tastes at all.
They dislike shops that accept payments in digital form or take orders by messaging.
Online platforms are the only places where goods can be seen and touched.
They tend to compare prices on phones first, and online sellers can often charge less.
They are unable to use messaging to place orders with any shop.
questions.explanation: Younger customers are "used to comparing prices on a phone", and online platforms "can offer lower prices". Shops that ignore this risk losing them; the other reasons are not in the passage or contradict it.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a shop that accepts digital payments and delivers within its own area?
options: It can now charge lower prices than any online platform, whatever its costs may be.
It will soon be forced to sell books and basic electronics instead of its present goods.
It has stopped serving regular customers who pay at the end of the month.
It is adapting to what online sellers offer while keeping the real advantages of being local.
It has given up trying to compete through trust built over time with regular customers.
questions.explanation: The successful retailers "cooperate with technology" through digital payments and local delivery while keeping their own strengths. Nothing suggests that they have abandoned regular customers, trust or their product range, or that they can undercut online platforms.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE according to the passage?
options: Buyers can judge the quality of clothes and furniture better from photographs than in person.
Online platforms close earlier in the evening than most neighbourhood stores do in towns.
Local shops always charge lower prices than online platforms because their costs are small.
A local shop may let a regular customer pay at the end of the month.
Every local shop that sold books and electronics has since gone out of business.
questions.explanation: The passage lists flexibility as an advantage: a store "may allow a regular customer to pay at the end of the month". The other statements are contradicted by the passage.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true according to the passage?
options: A shopkeeper's knowledge of regular customers can help in selling products.
Online platforms can offer lower prices because they sell in huge volumes.
Some local shops now take orders by means of messaging.
Technology has changed the way in which local businesses must compete.
Shops that sold books and electronics were among the best survivors.
questions.explanation: Shops selling books and basic electronics are named among those that closed, so calling them the most successful survivors contradicts the passage. The other statements are supported by the text.

questions.stem: The author's attitude towards local retailers is best described as:
questions.explanation: The author admits some shops closed and that threats remain, yet shows how many have adapted successfully. That is realistic and mildly hopeful.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most similar in meaning to the word “flexibility” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: In "A third is flexibility", the word refers to a shop's ability to adjust to customers' needs, which is closest to adaptability.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most opposite in meaning to the word “complicated” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: A complicated picture is one with many tangled parts; the opposite is a simple one.

paragraphs: Cities are usually hotter than the countryside around them. Concrete, brick and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, while the lack of trees means there is little shade and little moisture to cool the air. The result is called the urban heat island, and in summer it can make a city several degrees warmer than the nearby villages. Hot nights are especially harmful because the body gets no chance to recover from the day's heat.

One answer is to put plants where buildings now stand. Rooftop gardens and green walls shade the surfaces beneath them, and the water that leaves their leaves cools the air much as sweat cools the skin. A building with a green roof also needs less air conditioning, which saves electricity. Such roofs soak up rainwater too, reducing the flooding that follows a heavy shower in a city with few open spaces.

However, green roofs are not cheap. They need a strong structure to carry the soil, a waterproof layer to protect the building, and regular care so that the plants stay healthy. For this reason, owners of old buildings often hesitate. Some cities have tried to change that by offering reduced property taxes to owners who install them, or by making green roofs compulsory on new public buildings.

Planting is not a complete solution. Light-coloured paint on roofs and roads, which reflects sunlight, is cheaper and works faster, and open parks help to cool whole neighbourhoods. The best plan combines several measures, chosen to suit the climate and the budget of each city.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the main idea of the passage?
options: Light-coloured paint is a better answer to urban heat than any other measure.
Green roofs are the only effective way of fighting the heat of crowded cities in summer.
Air conditioning should be banned in cities so that electricity can be saved.
Cities are hotter than villages because they have too many people living in them today.
Cities can be cooled in several ways, and green roofs are one useful but costly choice.
questions.explanation: The passage explains why cities are hot, describes green roofs and their cost, and concludes that several measures should be combined. The other statements are too narrow, extreme or unsupported.

questions.stem: Why are hot nights especially harmful in a city?
options: Surfaces keep releasing stored heat after dark, leaving people little chance to recover.
Rainwater collected on roofs becomes warm and spreads through the streets.
Nearby villages send their hot air into the city after sunset every day.
Air conditioning stops working at night when the demand for electricity is highest.
Trees give off extra moisture at night, which makes the air very uncomfortable.
questions.explanation: Concrete, brick and asphalt "release it slowly at night", and hot nights are harmful because "the body gets no chance to recover". Combining the two explains the harm.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred about owners of old buildings?
options: They dislike plants because roots always damage the waterproof layer of a roof.
They are legally required to install green roofs on every public building.
They hesitate chiefly because installing and keeping a green roof is costly.
They already receive lower property taxes in every city that has green roofs.
They prefer air conditioning because it saves more electricity than plants do.
questions.explanation: The passage says green roofs are "not cheap" and that "for this reason" owners of old buildings often hesitate. Cost is therefore the main cause; the other statements are not supported.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about cities that reduce property taxes for owners of green roofs?
options: They have made green roofs compulsory on all private buildings in the city.
They have stopped worrying about flooding after heavy showers of rain.
They expect green roofs to remove the need for parks in every district.
They hope to encourage green roofs by easing the cost for owners.
They believe that green roofs are cheaper than light-coloured paint.
questions.explanation: Owners hesitate because green roofs are costly, and the tax reduction is offered "to change that", so it is meant to ease the cost. The passage says nothing to support the other statements.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE according to the passage?
options: Parks cool only the single building that stands beside them.
Green roofs cause flooding after a heavy shower in crowded cities.
Green roofs increase the amount of air conditioning that a building needs.
The urban heat island is strongest during the winter months.
Light-coloured paint is cheaper and acts faster than green roofs.
questions.explanation: The passage says that light-coloured paint "is cheaper and works faster". The other statements reverse or ignore what the passage says.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true according to the passage?
options: Water leaving leaves cools the air in the way that sweat cools skin.
Green roofs can soak up rainwater from heavy showers in crowded areas.
Open parks can help to cool whole neighbourhoods of a city.
Plants on a roof shade the surface beneath them.
Cities that use green roofs have made them compulsory on every new building.
questions.explanation: Only some cities have made green roofs compulsory, and only on new public buildings, so the keyed statement goes beyond the passage. The other statements are all given in the text.

questions.stem: The tone of the passage is best described as:
questions.explanation: The author explains a problem, presents a remedy with its costs, and recommends a mix of measures, without strong emotion. That is informative and balanced.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most similar in meaning to the word “compulsory” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: In "making green roofs compulsory", compulsory means required by rule, which is closest to mandatory.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most opposite in meaning to the word “harmful” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: Hot nights are described as harmful; the opposite is beneficial.

paragraphs: Online banking has made it possible to pay bills, transfer money and check balances without visiting a branch. Convenient as this is, it has also attracted criminals, who have found that it is often easier to trick a customer than to break into a bank's computer system. Most successful frauds today do not rely on advanced hacking. They rely on persuading people to hand over their own information.

A common method is the fake message. A customer receives a text or an email that appears to come from the bank, warning that the account will be blocked unless a link is clicked at once. The link leads to a copy of the bank's website, and anything typed there goes straight to the fraudster. Another method is the phone call, in which a caller pretends to be a bank officer and asks for a one-time password in order to stop a suspicious payment. Both methods depend on creating urgency, because a worried person acts quickly and thinks less.

Banks repeat a simple rule: no genuine officer will ever ask for a password, a PIN or a one-time code. A customer who has shared such details should contact the bank immediately, since a fast report gives the bank a better chance of stopping the transfer. Customers should also type the bank's address themselves, instead of following links, and should keep their mobile software updated.

Technology can improve protection, but it cannot replace caution. A strong password is of little use if it is told to a stranger on the phone. The most dependable security system is a customer who pauses, doubts an unexpected request, and checks it through the bank's official number.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best title for the passage?
options: The Advanced Hacking Methods Used by Criminals Against Bank Computers
How Software Updates Remove the Need for Caution Among Users
Why Banks Should Stop Offering Online Services to All Their Customers
The Role of Bank Officers in Catching Fraudsters Who Use Phones
Online Banking Fraud: How It Works and How Customers Can Resist It
questions.explanation: The passage describes common tricks used by fraudsters and the habits that protect customers. The other titles describe topics the passage does not discuss, or contradict it.

questions.stem: Why do fraudsters try to create a sense of urgency?
options: Bank systems automatically block accounts when messages are not answered quickly by customers.
Urgent messages are harder for banks to trace than ordinary messages are.
Customers who respond slowly are always asked for more personal information by fraudsters.
A worried person acts quickly and thinks less, so the trick works better.
Fraudsters are themselves worried that the bank will soon catch them out.
questions.explanation: Both methods "depend on creating urgency, because a worried person acts quickly and thinks less". The other explanations are not supported by the passage.

questions.stem: A person receives a call from someone claiming to be a bank officer who wants a one-time code. What can be inferred about the caller?
options: The call is safe as long as it is about stopping a suspicious payment on the account.
The bank has probably blocked the account and needs the code to unlock it.
The customer should give the code only if the caller sounds polite and well informed.
The caller is genuine if he knows the customer's name, address and account number.
The caller is probably not genuine, as no real officer asks for such a code.
questions.explanation: The passage says that "no genuine officer will ever ask for a password, a PIN or a one-time code", and fraudsters use calls of exactly this kind. The caller is therefore very likely a fraudster.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a customer who has shared a one-time code and reports it to the bank at once?
options: The fraudster will be unable to use a copy of the website again.
The bank will have to update its mobile software before it can act.
The customer will be blamed for the fraud, since the code was shared.
The transfer will certainly be stopped, whatever the delay in reporting it to the bank.
The bank may still be able to stop the transfer, because a fast report improves its chances.
questions.explanation: A customer who has shared details should report "immediately, since a fast report gives the bank a better chance of stopping the transfer". The passage speaks of a better chance, not a certainty.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE according to the passage?
options: A strong password gives full protection even if it is told to a stranger.
Many frauds depend on persuading customers to hand over their own details.
Most frauds begin with criminals breaking into a bank's computer system.
Fake websites are easy to spot because they look different from the bank's site.
Genuine bank officers sometimes ask for a PIN to stop a suspicious payment.
questions.explanation: The passage says that most successful frauds "rely on persuading people to hand over their own information". The other statements contradict the text.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true according to the passage?
options: A fast report gives the bank a better chance of stopping a transfer.
Customers are advised to type the bank's address themselves.
Fake messages often say that the account will be blocked unless a link is clicked.
A password is of little use if it is told to a stranger.
Most frauds today depend on advanced hacking of bank computers.
questions.explanation: The passage states that most successful frauds "do not rely on advanced hacking", so the keyed statement is false. The other statements all appear in the passage.

questions.stem: The tone of the passage is best described as:
questions.explanation: The author warns about fraud and gives clear, usable advice. That is cautionary and practical rather than resentful, relaxed, impersonal or sorrowful.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most similar in meaning to the word “genuine” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: In "no genuine officer", genuine means real, not pretending, which is closest to authentic.

questions.stem: Which of the following words is most opposite in meaning to the word “dependable” as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: Dependable means able to be relied on; the opposite is unreliable.

paragraphs: Central banks are often described as guardians of price stability, yet their influence over everyday prices is (1) ______ rather than direct. A rise in the policy rate does not (2) ______ the cost of vegetables or fuel; it merely makes borrowing dearer, in the hope that households and firms will (3) ______ their spending. Whether that hope is fulfilled depends largely on expectations. If people believe that inflation will remain low, they moderate their wage demands and price increases, and the outcome tends to (4) ______ the belief. If trust weakens, (5) ______, even a sharp rise in rates may fail to restrain prices, since businesses assume that costs will keep climbing. For this reason, a credible commitment is as important as any particular rate, and some economists argue that the central bank's most (6) ______ asset is not its balance sheet but its reputation. An institution that is believed needs to act less often, and when it must act, it can do so with smaller and less disruptive steps.

questions.stem: Select the most appropriate word to fill blank (1).
questions.explanation: The phrase "rather than direct" calls for its opposite, and the passage goes on to show that policy works only through borrowing costs and expectations; that is, it is indirect.

questions.stem: Select the most appropriate word to fill blank (2).

questions.stem: Select the most appropriate word to fill blank (3).
questions.explanation: Dearer borrowing is meant to hold spending back, so the verb must mean to restrain: curb. The other verbs would either mean the opposite or make no sense with "spending".

questions.stem: Select the most appropriate word to fill blank (4).
questions.explanation: After "tends to" the plain base form is required, so confirm is the only grammatical choice, and it also gives the sense that the outcome bears out the belief.

questions.stem: Select the most appropriate word to fill blank (5).

questions.stem: Select the most appropriate word to fill blank (6).

The mechanisation of farming did not (2) ______ in permanent mass unemployment; labour moved, over decades, into manufacturing and services. But the comparison has limits, (3) ______ earlier machines replaced muscle, whereas present systems increasingly imitate judgement. Whether the pattern will repeat is therefore uncertain. What seems clear is that the transition will be uneven: some regions and age groups will (4) ______ far more than others. Retraining programmes can help, provided they are (5) ______ to actual local demand for skills rather than copied from some distant model. Policy that merely hopes the market will (6) ______ the gap is likely to leave many workers waiting, and waiting, for a recovery that never quite reaches them. Reassurance drawn only from the past is thin comfort for a worker who is fifty and unemployed today.

Food, fuel and clothing all carry prices that rise when supplies tighten, but the tap in most homes delivers an essential good at a price that scarcely changes. In many cities, households pay a (2) ______ fee that bears little relation to the cost of treating and delivering what they use, so there is scant reason to economise. Raising charges is the obvious remedy, but it is politically (3) ______ because water is also a necessity, and steep bills fall hardest on the poor. It cannot, (5) ______, succeed unless leaks are repaired, for a network that loses a third of its supply before it reaches any tap will remain unsustainable, however carefully customers conserve. Conservation by consumers, in short, is no (6) ______ for sound management by suppliers.

questions.stem: Select the most appropriate word to fill blank (2).

questions.stem: Select the most appropriate word to fill blank (3).

questions.stem: Select the most appropriate word to fill blank (4).

questions.stem: Select the most appropriate word to fill blank (5).

Rules written too (1) ______ may stifle experiments that would have widened access to credit; rules written too loosely invite the kind of reckless lending that regulation exists to prevent. questions.stem: Select the most appropriate word to fill blank (2).

questions.explanation: After the preposition “at” the series “reducing ..., improving ...” needs a third gerund, so “and encouraging” keeps the structure parallel.

questions.explanation: “Insist” takes the preposition “on” before a gerund: “insisted on being given access”. The other prepositions are not used with “insist” in this way.

questions.explanation: The inverted “Had ... tested” is a third conditional about the unreal past, so the result clause needs “would have been discovered”.

Seldom THE COUNCIL HAS faced such a sharply divided public response as the one over the proposed bypass.
questions.explanation: A negative adverb such as “Seldom” at the start of a sentence requires inversion of the auxiliary and subject, and the present perfect is completed by “faced”: “Seldom has the council faced ...”.

questions.explanation: A multiple comparison of equal degree is built as “twice as large as”, with the positive adjective between the two “as” words.
